questions.prompt: Why is memory the only recovery path for certain artifacts?
options: Disk forensics tools are less mature
Anything that deliberately avoided the filesystem -- reflectively loaded assemblies, in-memory payloads -- has no on-disk representation to recover
Memory is easier to acquire than disk
questions.explanation: This is why acquisition order matters beyond volatility: a host powered off before capture loses the payload itself permanently, with no alternative source.

questions.prompt: Which Volatility plugin most directly extracts an injected payload?
options: windows.malfind --dump, which identifies injected regions and writes them out in one step
questions.explanation: Because malfind already locates private, executable, unbacked regions, adding --dump produces the payload without manual reconstruction.

questions.prompt: Why might a file encrypted at rest be recoverable in plaintext from memory?
options: A file must be decrypted to be used, so while it is open the plaintext exists in memory
Windows stores decryption keys in the page file
Encrypted files are never loaded into memory
questions.explanation: This applies to encrypted archives an attacker staged, protected documents, and configuration files holding credentials.

questions.prompt: How should memory-recovered content be characterized in reporting?
options: As equivalent to a disk-recovered file
As a sample of the artifact rather than the artifact, since only cached or mapped pages are present and completeness cannot be proven
As identical to the original in all cases
questions.explanation: Partial and potentially stale content requires explicit provenance and confidence language rather than being presented as a complete recovered file.
